resources.string: "[Principle] Binary morphological operations act on sets. The grayscale image is first segmented into a binary image A (foreground white 255 / background black 0) by Otsu\'s method with an automatically computed global threshold, serving as the input baseline for all subsequent binary morphological operations.\n[Implementation] OpenCV cv::threshold(THRESH_BINARY | THRESH_OTSU).\n[Note] Items ② ~ ⑥ below all operate on the same binary image, with a uniform 5×5 rectangular structuring element."

"[Principle] Erosion is the set of all translations z such that the structuring element B, when translated by z, is entirely contained in set A; it shrinks the image boundary inward and removes small protrusions.
[Eq. 3-9] A ⊖ B = { z | (B)_z ⊆ A }
 That is, z belongs to the erosion result when the translated structuring element still falls entirely inside the target region.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 rectangle.
[Effect] The white foreground shrinks, thin connections are broken, and isolated white points smaller than the structuring element are removed."

"[Principle] Opening = erosion followed by dilation; it smooths object contours, breaks narrow connections, and removes small spikes and isolated points while keeping the overall size basically unchanged.
[Eq. 3-15] A ∘ B = (A ⊖ B) ⊕ B
[Eq. 3-16] A ∘ B = ∪ { (B)_z | (B)_z ⊆ A }
 That is, the union of all translations of the structuring element that fit entirely inside A.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 rectangle.
[Effect] Small white noise is wiped out while the shape of large targets is preserved."

"[Principle] Closing = dilation followed by erosion; it bridges narrow breaks and holes and smooths contours while keeping the overall size basically unchanged.
[Eq. 3-17] A • B = (A ⊕ B) ⊖ B
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 rectangle.
[Effect] Small black holes and thin gaps are filled, and the connectivity of the white main body is enhanced."

"[Principle] Erosion and dilation are duals of each other: eroding the target set equals dilating its complement (background) and then complementing again, and vice versa.
[Eq. 3-13] (A ⊖ B)^c = A^c ⊕ B̂
[Eq. 3-14] (A ⊕ B)^c = A^c ⊖ B̂
[Verification] This item inverts the input (foreground/background swapped) and applies erosion, then compares it with the complement of direct dilation; the two should coincide.
[Note] This demo outputs the inverted-erosion result, which can be compared with the ③ dilation image to observe the duality."
"[Principle] The same Otsu binarization result as in Sec. 3.2, serving as the input baseline for items ② ~ ⑧ on this page.\n[Implementation] OpenCV cv::threshold(THRESH_BINARY | THRESH_OTSU)."

"[Principle] Inner edge = the original set minus its erosion, yielding a ring of boundary pixels on the inner side of the target.
[Eq. 3-20] β(A) = A − (A ⊖ B)
[Eq. 3-21] β(A) = A − ∪ { (B)_z | (B)_z ⊆ A }
[Parameters] Structuring element: 3×3 rectangle (boundary width 1 pixel).
[Effect] The inner-edge contour of the white target."

"[Principle] Outer edge = the dilated target minus the original set, yielding a ring of boundary pixels on the outer side of the target.
[Eq. 3-22] β_ext(A) = (A ⊕ B) − A
[Parameters] Structuring element: 3×3 rectangle.
[Effect] The outer-edge contour of the white target, complementary to the ② inner edge."

"[Principle] Morphological gradient = the dilation result minus the erosion result, covering both the inner and outer boundaries of the target with thicker and more complete edges; it is the binary special case of the grayscale morphological gradient (Eq. 3-46).
[Formula] Grad(A) = (A ⊕ B) − (A ⊖ B)
[Parameters] Structuring element: 3×3 rectangle.
[Effect] A complete double-edge contour band."

"[Principle] Starting from a point inside a hole, repeatedly dilate with the structuring element and intersect with the complement of A until convergence, thereby filling all holes inside A.
[Eq. 3-23] X_k = (X_{k−1} ⊕ B) ∩ A^c, k = 1, 2, …
 At convergence X_k = X_{k−1}, and the filled result = A ∪ X_k.
[Implementation] Flood-filling the complement from seeds on the image boundary (external background) and then inverting, an engineering implementation equivalent to the Eq. 3-23 iteration.
[Effect] The black holes inside the white target are completely filled."

"[Principle] The skeleton is the minimal centerline representation of a target. Repeatedly erode and take the difference between each erosion and its opening; the union of all these differences yields the skeleton.
[Eq. 3-24] S(A) = ∪_{n=0}^{N} S_n(A)
[Eq. 3-25] S_n(A) = (A ⊖ nB) − [(A ⊖ nB) ∘ B]
[Eq. 3-26] Reconstruction: A = ∪_{n=0}^{N} (S_n(A) ⊕ nB)
[Eq. 3-27] (A ⊖ nB) denotes n successive erosions by the structuring element B.
[Eq. 3-28] N is the maximum number of erosions before A becomes the empty set.
[Effect] The white target is reduced to a single-pixel central skeleton line."

"[Principle] Thinning is a sequential algorithm for computing the skeleton: boundary pixels are peeled off round by round with a sequence of structuring elements via hit-or-miss transforms until the result no longer changes.
[Eq. 3-29] A ⊗ B = A − (A * B)
 where * is the hit-or-miss transform.
[Eq. 3-30] A ⊗ {B} = ((…((A ⊗ B_1) ⊗ B_2)…) ⊗ B_n)
 The structuring element sequence {B_1…B_n} is applied in order and iterated repeatedly.
[Eq. 3-31] The thinned result satisfies: thinning A ⊗ {B} once more causes no change (convergence).
[Implementation] Hand-written Zhang-Suen sequential thinning (two-pass scanning that deletes boundary points, corresponding to the rotated structuring element sequence B1…B8 of Eq. 3-30).
[Effect] The target shrinks into thin lines without breaking, preserving topological connectivity."

"[Principle] Opening filters white (pepper) noise and closing filters black (salt) noise; cascading the two yields a morphological filter.
[Eq. 3-34] Opening then closing: (A ∘ B) • B
[Eq. 3-35] Closing then opening: (A • B) ∘ B
 This implementation follows Eq. 3-34.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 rectangle.
[Effect] Isolated noise points on the binary image are removed while the main shape stays unchanged."

"[Principle] No processing; the original grayscale image is shown directly as the reference baseline for items ② ~ ⑤ (basic grayscale morphological operations).\n[Note] Grayscale morphology no longer treats the image as a set but as a two-dimensional grayscale function f(x,y); the structuring element b(x,y) is a small sub-image function, and the operations take the maximum/minimum over pixel neighborhoods."

"[Principle] Grayscale erosion = taking the minimum over the neighborhood defined by the structuring element; the output image darkens, and bright details smaller than the structuring element (high grayscale peaks) are removed.
[Eq. 3-36] (f ⊖ b)(x, y) = min { f(x + x′, y + y′) − b(x′, y′) }
 (x′, y′) ∈ D_b (the domain of the structuring element), fully contained in the domain of f after translation.
[Eq. 3-37] For a flat structuring element (b = 0) it simplifies to: (f ⊖ b)(x, y) = min_{(x′,y′)∈D_b} f(x + x′, y + y′)
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 ellipse (flat).
[Effect] The image darkens overall and bright points are smoothed away."

"[Principle] Grayscale dilation = taking the maximum over the neighborhood; the output image brightens, and dark details (low grayscale valleys) are filled.
[Eq. 3-38] (f ⊕ b)(x, y) = max { f(x − x′, y − y′) + b(x′, y′) }
 (x′, y′) ∈ D_b.
[Eq. 3-39] For a flat structuring element it simplifies to: (f ⊕ b)(x, y) = max_{(x′,y′)∈D_b} f(x − x′, y − y′)
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 ellipse (flat).
[Effect] The image brightens overall and dark pits are filled, dual to ② erosion."

"[Principle] Grayscale opening = erosion followed by dilation; it removes bright details smaller than the structuring element (bright points, spikes, bright noise) while preserving the overall grayscale contour.
[Eq. 3-42] f ∘ b = (f ⊖ b) ⊕ b
[Eq. 3-43] Geometric interpretation: push the structuring element “upward from below” against the surface of f; the upper envelope of its center-point trajectory is the opening result.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 ellipse (flat).
[Effect] Small bright protrusions and noise are filtered out, while dark structures are unaffected."

"[Principle] Grayscale closing = dilation followed by erosion; it removes dark details smaller than the structuring element (dark points, valleys, dark noise) while preserving the overall grayscale contour.
[Eq. 3-44] f • b = (f ⊕ b) ⊖ b
[Eq. 3-45] Geometric interpretation: press the structuring element “downward from above” onto the surface of f; the lower envelope of its center-point trajectory is the closing result.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 ellipse (flat).
[Effect] Small dark ravines and noise are filled, while bright structures are unaffected, dual to ④ opening."

"[Principle] No processing; the original grayscale image is shown directly as the reference baseline for items ② ~ ⑦ (grayscale morphological processing algorithms) on this page.\n[Note] The algorithms below are all composed on the grayscale image from opening/closing/dilation/erosion primitives."

"[Principle] Dilation minus erosion gives the morphological gradient, with the strongest response at grayscale discontinuities (edges); it is the morphological approach to image edge detection.
[Eq. 3-46] Grad(f) = (f ⊕ b) − (f ⊖ b)
[Parameters] Structuring element: 3×3 ellipse (a small kernel gives finer edges).
[Effect] Image edges are highlighted while flat regions output zero."

"[Principle] Alternating opening and closing in series filters both positive and negative impulse noise, realizing morphological smoothing.
[Eq. 3-47] O C(f) = (f ∘ b) • b (opening then closing)
[Eq. 3-48] C O(f) = (f • b) ∘ b (closing then opening, see item ④)
 This item follows Eq. 3-47.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 ellipse.
[Effect] The image becomes smoother, with isolated bright/dark noise points suppressed at the same time."

"[Principle] Closing then opening, the mirror order of ③; it works better on images dominated by dark noise, and combining the two can further reduce bias.
[Eq. 3-48] C O(f) = (f • b) ∘ b
[Parameters] Structuring element: 5×5 ellipse.
[Effect] Smoothing is close to ③ with slight differences in edge preservation — compare them side by side."

"[Principle] Top-hat = the original image minus its opening, used to extract details smaller than the structuring element and brighter than their surroundings (bright points, small peaks); it can also correct uneven illumination.
[Eq. 3-49] TopHat(f) = f − (f ∘ b)
[Parameters] Structuring element: 15×15 ellipse (a large kernel extracts bright details more fully).
[Effect] Bright small targets and details are separated out, and the background tends to zero."

"[Principle] Bottom-hat = the closing minus the original image, used to extract details smaller than the structuring element and darker than their surroundings (dark points, small valleys); it is the dual transform of the top-hat.
[Formula] BotHat(f) = (f • b) − f
[Parameters] Structuring element: 15×15 ellipse.
[Effect] Dark small targets and details are separated out, and the background tends to zero."

"[Principle] The top-hat extracts bright details and the bottom-hat extracts dark details; adding and subtracting them from the original image enhances both positive and negative weak details simultaneously, followed by normalization to the full grayscale range — a typical engineering application of joint top-hat/bottom-hat contrast enhancement (e.g. shadow or low-contrast region enhancement).
[Formula] Enhance(f) = stretch[ f + TopHat(f) − BotHat(f) ]
 where TopHat is as in Eq. 3-49, BotHat(f) = (f • b) − f,
 and stretch is the [min, max] → [0, 255] normalization.
[Parameters] Structuring element: 15×15 ellipse.
[Effect] Bright and dark details are enhanced together with a marked improvement in overall contrast; compare with the ⑤ top-hat result."

"[Principle] No processing; the original image is shown directly as the reference baseline for items ② ~ ⑥ (thresholding segmentation algorithms) on this page.\n[Note] Grayscale thresholding is the simplest image segmentation method: pixels are divided into foreground/background classes by gray level, and the key lies in choosing a suitable threshold T."

"[Principle] The image is divided into two parts by a single manually specified threshold T: pixels with gray level greater than T form one class, and the rest form the other.
[Eq. 4-1] g(x,y) = 1, f(x,y) > T; g(x,y) = 0, f(x,y) ≤ T
[Parameters] T = 128 (fixed demo value).
[Characteristics] Simple and fast, but relies on manual experience and is unstable under illumination changes."

"[Principle] Starting from an initial threshold, the threshold is repeatedly updated from the means of the two classes until convergence, yielding a near-optimal global threshold.
[Eq. 4-3] T_{k+1} = (μ1 + μ2) / 2
 μ1 and μ2 are the gray means of the two classes partitioned by T_k; stop when |T_{k+1} − T_k| is small enough.
[Implementation] The initial T₀ takes the global mean; iterate until the threshold change is below 0.5.
[Characteristics] Automatic thresholding; near-optimal for images with bimodal histograms."

"[Principle] Otsu's method: scan all possible thresholds; the one that maximizes the between-class variance σB² of the foreground/background classes is the optimal segmentation threshold.
[Eq. 4-4] σB²(t) = ω1(t)·ω2(t)·[μ1(t) − μ2(t)]²
[Eq. 4-5/4-6] ω1, ω2: the probabilities (frequencies) of the two classes.
[Eq. 4-7/4-8] μ1, μ2: the mean gray levels of the two classes.
[Eq. 4-9/4-10] T* = arg max σB²(t), equivalent to the minimum within-class variance criterion.
[Implementation] OpenCV cv::threshold(THRESH_OTSU) with global automatic optimization.
[Characteristics] The most commonly used automatic thresholding method; stable when target and background gray levels differ clearly."

"[Principle] Under uneven illumination a global threshold cannot accommodate both bright and dark areas. The threshold T of Eq. 4-2 is localized: each pixel's threshold is determined dynamically by the mean (or weighted sum) of the pixels in its neighborhood window.
[Localized Eq. 4-2] T(x,y) = neighborhood mean(x,y) − C
[Parameters] Neighborhood window 31×31, correction constant C = 10.
[Implementation] OpenCV cv::adaptiveThreshold(ADAPTIVE_THRESH_MEAN_C).
[Characteristics] Adapts to gradual illumination changes; suitable for binarization in shadow or unevenly lit scenes."

"[Principle] A generalization of Eq. 4-1: multiple thresholds T1 < T2 < … cut the gray axis into several intervals, each taken as one class of region — suitable for images with many gray levels of target and background.
[Formula] g(x,y) = k, if T_{k−1} < f(x,y) ≤ T_k (k = 1…M)
[Implementation] Multiple thresholds are selected automatically from histogram peaks, and each interval is mapped to a different gray level.
[Characteristics] One segmentation yields multiple regions — a direct extension of single-threshold binary segmentation."

"[Principle] The Otsu segmentation mask is overlaid on the original image: the foreground keeps its original gray levels while the background is darkened with a red highlight, intuitively showing where the threshold-extracted target regions lie in the original image.\n[Note] An engineering visualization of segmentation results, useful for checking whether the threshold is well chosen.\n[Effect] The segmented foreground regions are marked in red as an overlay."

"[Principle] No processing; the original image is shown directly as the reference baseline for items ② ~ ⑦ (edge-detection segmentation algorithms) on this page.\n[Note] Edges are locations of abrupt grayscale change; edge-based segmentation first detects edges and then links them into closed boundaries, thereby partitioning the image into regions."

"[Principle] The Roberts cross-difference operator: differencing along the diagonal directions in a 2×2 neighborhood; a small template and fast computation with high edge localization accuracy, but sensitive to noise.
[Eq. 4-18] G[f(x,y)] ≈ |Gx| + |Gy| (gradient magnitude approximation of Eq. 4-14)
[Eq. 4-19] Hx = [−1 0; 0 1], Hy = [0 −1; 1 0]
[Effect] Thin and bright diagonal edges."

"[Principle] The Sobel operator introduces an averaging factor into the difference template: weighted neighborhood averaging followed by differencing, sharpening edges while suppressing noise.
[Eq. 4-20] Hx = [−1 0 1; −2 0 2; −1 0 1], Hy is its transpose
[Magnitude] G ≈ |Gx| + |Gy|
[Parameters] Kernel size 3×3.
[Effect] Thicker and brighter edges; better noise robustness than Roberts."

"[Principle] The Prewitt operator follows the same idea as Sobel but with all averaging weights set to 1 — a pure mean-difference template.
[Eq. 4-21] Hx = [−1 0 1; −1 0 1; −1 0 1], Hy is its transpose
[Eq. 4-22] G ≈ |Gx| + |Gy|
[Effect] Smooth edges with some noise suppression, slightly thicker than Sobel."

"[Principle] The Laplacian is an isotropic second-derivative operator with zero crossings at edges; extremely sensitive to grayscale changes, and to noise as well.
[Eq. 4-26] ∇²f = f(i+1,j) + f(i−1,j) + f(i,j+1) + f(i,j−1) − 4f(i,j)
[Eq. 4-27/4-28] 4-neighborhood / 8-neighborhood discrete templates.
[Effect] Double-edge response; isolated noise points are strongly amplified."

"[Principle] The Marr-Hildreth operator: Gaussian smoothing for denoising first, then the Laplacian — overcoming the noise sensitivity of the Laplacian; edges are found by detecting zero crossings of the second derivative.
[Eq. 4-29] ∇²G(x,y) (LoG kernel, Mexican-hat shaped)
[Eq. 4-30] g = f * Gσ (Gaussian smoothing)
[Eq. 4-31] ∇²(f * G) = f * ∇²G (convolution and differentiation commute)
[Eq. 4-32/4-33] LoG discrete template and zero-crossing criterion.
[Parameters] Kernel size 5×5, σ = 1.5.
[Effect] Well-closed edges and strong noise robustness."

"[Principle] Edge detection yields discrete edge points; edge closing and contour tracing are required to form region boundaries and complete the segmentation: a morphological dilate-erode closing first bridges the gaps in the Canny edges, then outer contours are extracted and filled as regions.\n[Pipeline] Canny edges → morphological closing → contour extraction (cv::findContours) → contour filling into regions\n[Effect] Outputs a segmented region map enclosed by closed boundaries, completing the full “edge-to-region” segmentation chain."

"[Principle] Region growing (4.4.1): starting from seed points, pixels similar to the seed in property (gray level) and spatially adjacent are continuously merged into the region until no pixel satisfies the condition, producing a connected segmented region.
[Formula] R = ∪ R_k, where R_k satisfies: P(R_k) = TRUE and for adjacent regions P(R_i ∪ R_j) = FALSE
 P is the gray-similarity criterion: |f(p) − f(seed)| ≤ T.
[Parameters] Seed at the image center, similarity threshold T = 16.
[Effect] A single connected region (white) grown from the center; the red dot marks the seed."

"[Principle] Seed selection principle (4.4.1): seeds should lie at stable interior positions of regions. This item selects seeds automatically from histogram peaks — each peak of the gray distribution represents the typical gray level of a region; peak points are taken as seeds and grown in parallel, achieving automatic multi-region segmentation.\n[Parameters] Similarity threshold T = 16; the number of seeds is determined automatically from the number of histogram peaks.\n[Effect] Multiple connected regions of different gray levels are grown simultaneously and pseudo-color labeled."

"[Principle] Region split-and-merge (4.4.2): a top-down strategy opposite to growing. The image is repeatedly split into four sub-blocks (quadtree); blocks failing the homogeneity criterion keep splitting; then adjacent sub-blocks satisfying the merge criterion are merged, yielding the final segmentation.\n[Criterion] Split: split into four when the within-block gray variance > threshold; merge: merge adjacent blocks when their mean gray difference < threshold.\n[Effect] Outputs a quadtree block-region map where block boundaries are the segmentation boundaries, balancing global and local characteristics."

"[Principle] Connected component labeling: on the binarized image, white pixels that are 4/8-connected are grouped into the same region with a unified label; each labeled region is an independent segmented target.
[Formula] R_i ∩ R_j = ∅ (i≠j), ∪ R_i = the foreground set
[Implementation] Otsu binarization → cv::connectedComponents labeling → pseudo-coloring by label.
[Effect] Each connected target appears in a different color, allowing target counting and area statistics."

"[Principle] The watershed algorithm (4.4.3): view the grayscale image as a topographic surface with gray level as altitude. Water is “poured” from markers, gathering in basins and damming at confluences; the dams are the segmentation boundaries — solving region segmentation of adhered targets.\n[Pipeline] Marker extraction (distance transform + threshold) → cv::watershed flooding → boundary dam extraction\n[Effect] Adhered targets are separated by dams; outputs a watershed result with region coloring + white segmentation boundaries."

"[Principle] The active contour model (Snake, Eq. 4-40): a parametric curve v(s) is initialized near the target and deforms under the combined action of internal energy (keeping the curve smooth) and image energy (attracting the curve toward edges); when the energy is minimized the curve stops at the target boundary, completing the segmentation.
[Eq. 4-40] E = ∫ [ α|v′(s)|² + β|v″(s)|² ] ds + E_img(v(s))
[Eq. 4-41] The first and second terms are internal energy: α controls elasticity (stretch resistance), β controls rigidity (bending resistance).
[Eq. 4-42~4-43] Discretization: N points on the curve, energy in summation form.
[Eq. 4-44] E_img = −|∇I|: points of large image gradient have low energy, attracting the contour.
[Eq. 4-45] ∇I is Gaussian-smoothed to widen the edge attraction range.
[Implementation] The Williams-Shah greedy algorithm searches the minimum-energy candidate within a neighborhood window point by point.
[Effect] The initial circular contour converges and adheres near the target edge."

"[Principle] In the internal energy (Eq. 4-41), the weights α and β determine the smoothness of the contour: large α suppresses stretching and uneven spacing; large β suppresses bending and sharp corners. This item demonstrates side by side the differences in convergence shape under different α/β combinations.\n[Eq. 4-41] E_int = α|v′(s)|² + β|v″(s)|²\n[Effect] Corner jitter with low β and over-smoothing with high β can be observed."

"[Principle] The basic Snake has a limited convergence radius and cannot reach a target too far from the initial contour. Cohen\'s balloon model adds an isotropic balloon force to the energy: continuous expansion (or contraction) along the contour normal drives the curve across flat gray regions, and the image energy stops it at the target edge.\n[Formula] E = E_int + E_img + k·(normal expansion term)\n[Effect] Starting from a contour far away from the target, it still expands and converges to the edge."

"[Principle] The geodesic active contour GAC (Eq. 4-46) multiplies the balloon force by the edge stopping function g = 1/(1+|∇Gσ*f|): in flat regions g≈1 and the balloon force advances at full speed, while at strong edges g→0 and the contour stops automatically — solving the problem of the plain balloon force crossing weak edges.
[Eq. 4-46] ∂C/∂t = g·|C|·N − (∇g)·N
 The first term is the g-modulated normal advancing force, and the second is the edge attraction term.
[Implementation] Within the greedy Snake framework, the balloon force coefficient is modulated by 1/(1+20g).
[Effect] The contour advances quickly in flat regions and stops precisely at edges."

"[Principle] The Chan-Vese region-based active contour (Eq. 4-47): instead of relying on gradient edges, the curve evolves by the criterion that “the gray levels inside and outside the contour should each be uniform”: the image is divided into the region inside the contour (mean c1) and the region outside (mean c2); at minimum energy the curve is the segmentation boundary.
[Eq. 4-47] E(c1,c2,C) = ∫_inside(f−c1)² + ∫_outside(f−c2)² + ν·Length(C)
[Implementation] The level set is simplified to alternating region-label updates: c1/c2 take the means inside/outside the contour, pixels are re-classified per the energy criterion, and iteration runs to convergence.
[Effect] Segments targets with weak or no clear edges, complementing gradient-based Snakes."
